html:
General Zia-ul-Haq ruled Pakistan from 1977 until his death in 1988. He made Islamic law part of the state and made Pakistan the base for the war against the Soviets in Afghanistan. Both choices shaped the country long after him.

He was born in 1924 at Jalandhar in Punjab, the son of a clerk, and served in the British Indian Army. Zulfikar Ali Bhutto made him army chief in 1976 over the heads of senior generals, thinking him harmless.

On 5 July 1977, during protests over a rigged election, Zia took power and promised a vote within ninety days. It was not held. Bhutto was hanged in 1979.

To give his rule a basis he turned to religion. New laws set whipping, amputation and stoning as punishments for theft and adultery, though the harshest were not carried out. The blasphemy law was made far stricter. A religious tax was taken from bank accounts, and religious schools multiplied.

When the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan in December 1979, American and Saudi money poured in. Pakistan's military intelligence armed and trained the Afghan fighters (see Operation Cyclone). Three million refugees arrived (see Afghan refugees), and with them guns and heroin.

He died when his plane crashed in August 1988. The cause was never found.
sum: General Zia-ul-Haq ruled Pakistan from 1977 until his death in 1988. He made Islamic law part of the state and made Pakistan the base for the war against the Soviets in Afghanistan. Both choices shaped the country long after him.
